definition: The total duration of outages on the distribution network during the reporting period, expressed in hours. It is calculated by summing the hours of planned downtime and unplanned (forced) downtime recorded for the distribution network in the service area, so it should reconcile with the separately reported planned and unplanned downtime figures. A common pitfall is entering customer-hours or equipment-hours of interruption instead of hours of network downtime.

The total circuit length of the utility's distribution network, in kilometres (km). Include all medium-voltage and low-voltage overhead lines and underground cables owned and operated by the utility in the service area; exclude lines operating at transmission voltage, which are reported separately under Transmission Network Length. This input feeds the Distribution O&M Cost per km and Distribution Reliability KPIs, so an over- or under-stated length distorts cost-per-kilometre and outage-rate comparisons across utilities. A common pitfall is reporting route length rather than circuit length where several circuits share the same poles or trench.

The number of planned outage events on the distribution network during the reporting period, expressed as a count of events. Count only interruptions of distribution plant that were scheduled in advance (for example maintenance, upgrades or new connections) with customers notified beforehand; unplanned (forced) events are reported separately, and momentary interruptions of less than one minute are excluded by standard benchmarking convention. A common pitfall is counting a single planned job that is switched in several stages as multiple separate events.

The number of unplanned (forced) outage events on the distribution network during the reporting period, expressed as a count of events. Include only interruptions of distribution plant caused by faults, equipment failure, weather or third-party damage without advance notice; planned events are reported separately, and momentary interruptions of less than one minute are excluded by standard benchmarking convention. This input feeds the Distribution Reliability KPI, so consistent event counting is essential for year-on-year and cross-utility comparison. A common pitfall is including outages that originated in generation or transmission rather than in the distribution network itself.

The total installed capacity of distribution transformers in the service area, expressed in megavolt-amperes (MVA). Sum the nameplate ratings of all distribution (MV/LV) transformers in service, including pole-mounted, pad-mounted and ground-mounted units; exclude transmission grid or power-station transformers. This input feeds the Transformer Utilization Factor KPI, which compares peak demand against installed transformer capacity. A common pitfall is entering values in kVA instead of MVA — divide kVA nameplate totals by 1,000.

The average load on the power system over the reporting period, expressed in MWh per hour of the period (numerically equal to the average demand in MW). It should be derived as the total electricity delivered to the network (net, sent out) divided by the number of hours in the period, measured on the same basis as the peak load figure. This input feeds the Load Factor KPI, which compares average load with peak load to show how evenly the system is utilised. A common pitfall is entering the total annual energy in MWh rather than the hourly average, which inflates the value by several thousand times.

The maximum load on the power system during the reporting period, expressed in MWh for the peak hour (numerically equal to the peak demand in MW when measured over a one-hour interval). Report the highest coincident system peak for the service area measured at the sent-out (net) level, after station auxiliaries, rather than the sum of individual feeder or station peaks, which overstates the true system maximum. This input feeds the Load Factor KPI, so it must be measured on the same basis as the average load figure. A common pitfall is reporting an instantaneous peak in kW or MW, or a gross generation peak, instead of the net hourly system peak.

The total electricity billed to customers during the reporting period, expressed in MWh. Include all metered sales to residential, commercial, industrial and government customers in the service area, plus street lighting where it is billed; exclude the utility's own internal consumption and any unbilled or unmetered supply, which are captured as losses. This input feeds the Customer Consumption, Network Delivery Losses and Transmission Network Losses KPIs, so under-recorded sales directly overstate reported network losses. A common pitfall is entering values in kWh rather than MWh — divide kWh billing totals by 1,000.

The total number of hours in the reporting period, expressed in hours. For a full reporting year this is 8,760 hours (8,784 in a leap year); if data covers a shorter or different period, enter the actual number of hours in that period. This input feeds the Generator Availability Factor, Generator Forced Outage Indicator and Generator Planned Outage Indicator KPIs, which express generator outage and available hours as a share of total period hours. A common pitfall is misalignment between this figure and the period covered by the generation and outage data — all must relate to the same fiscal or calendar year.

The total number of customer interruptions from all supply interruptions during the reporting period, expressed as a count of customers. It is calculated by adding the customers affected by planned interruptions to the customers affected by unplanned (forced) interruptions, counting a customer once for every event that interrupts them rather than as unique customers. Momentary interruptions of less than one minute are excluded, consistent with the planned and unplanned inputs from which it is built. A common pitfall is expecting this to equal the number of distinct customers interrupted — it is a sum of customer-interruptions and can exceed the total customer base.

The total number of supply interruption events from all causes during the reporting period, expressed as a count of events. It is calculated by adding the number of planned interruption events to the number of unplanned (forced) interruption events. Momentary interruptions of less than one minute are excluded, consistent with the planned and unplanned inputs from which it is built. A common pitfall is any mismatch with the separately reported planned and unplanned event counts — the three figures must reconcile.

The total number of customers affected by planned supply interruptions during the reporting period, expressed as a count of customers. For each planned event (scheduled in advance with customers notified), count the customers whose supply was interrupted and sum across all events — a customer interrupted by three planned events counts three times; momentary interruptions of less than one minute are excluded by standard benchmarking convention. This input feeds the Planned SAIDI and Planned SAIFI KPIs, so accurate customer counts per event directly determine the utility's published reliability indices. A common pitfall is reporting unique customers rather than customer-interruptions, which understates the reliability indices.

The number of planned supply interruption events during the reporting period, expressed as a count of events. Count only interruptions that were scheduled in advance (for example for maintenance, network upgrades or new connections) with prior notice to customers; unplanned (forced) interruptions are reported separately, and momentary interruptions of less than one minute are excluded by standard benchmarking convention. This input feeds the Planned SAIFI KPI, so consistent event definitions are essential for comparability. A common pitfall is counting each switching stage of a single planned job as a separate event.

The total number of customers affected by unplanned (forced) supply interruptions during the reporting period, expressed as a count of customers. For each unplanned event — faults, equipment failure, weather, vegetation or third-party damage occurring without advance notice — count the customers whose supply was interrupted and sum across all events, counting a customer once per event; momentary interruptions of less than one minute are excluded by standard benchmarking convention. A common pitfall is reporting unique customers rather than customer-interruptions, or omitting events restored quickly by automatic reclosing that still lasted one minute or longer.

The number of unplanned (forced) supply interruption events during the reporting period, expressed as a count of events. Include only interruptions occurring without advance notice — faults, equipment failure, weather, vegetation or third-party damage; planned interruptions are reported separately, and momentary interruptions of less than one minute are excluded by standard benchmarking convention. A common pitfall is inconsistent treatment of a single fault with staged restoration — it should normally be counted as one event, not one per restoration step.

The electricity sold to customers supplied directly from the transmission network during the reporting period, expressed in MWh. Include only metered sales to customers connected at transmission voltage (typically large industrial or bulk-supply customers taking supply before the distribution network); sales delivered through the distribution network are captured under Electricity Sold to Customers. This input feeds the Transmission Network Losses KPI, allowing transmission losses to be separated from distribution losses. A common pitfall is double-counting these sales in both this input and the general electricity-sold figure, which understates reported losses.

The total number of outage events on the transmission network during the reporting period, expressed as a count of events. It is calculated by adding planned (scheduled) downtime events to unplanned (forced) downtime events recorded for the transmission network in the service area, so it should reconcile with the separately reported planned and unplanned figures. Utilities without a distinct transmission system (no network operating at transmission voltage) do not report this input. A common pitfall is including distribution-level outages in the transmission count.

The number of customers supplied directly from the transmission network, expressed as a count of customers. Count metered customer connection points at transmission voltage (typically large industrial or bulk-supply customers), not the wider population served downstream through the distribution network; utilities without a distinct transmission system do not report this input. A common pitfall is reporting the total customer base instead of only the transmission-connected customers, which for most Pacific utilities is a very small number.

The total circuit length of the utility's transmission network, in kilometres (km). Include all overhead lines and underground cables operating at transmission voltage that the utility owns and operates; distribution-voltage lines are reported separately under Distribution Network Length, and utilities with no distinct transmission system do not report this input. This input feeds the Transmission Reliability KPI, which normalises transmission outages by network length. A common pitfall is reporting route length rather than circuit length where double-circuit towers carry more than one circuit.

The total duration of planned outages on the transmission network during the reporting period, expressed in hours. Include only downtime that was scheduled in advance (for example for maintenance, inspections or construction); unplanned (forced) downtime is reported separately, and utilities without a distinct transmission system do not report this input. A common pitfall is reporting the elapsed duration of the whole work programme rather than the actual hours the transmission plant was out of service.
